facts.claim: The Bandcamp credits for 'Blessing' list Jacob Portrait as engineer at Clubhouse in Rhinebeck, NY, Samuel Acchione on guitar, John Heywood on bass and Tom Kelly on drums.
'Blessing' was the first single from God Save the Animals. It came out on May 23, 2022, before the album was announced.
The album God Save the Animals came out on September 23, 2022 on Domino. It was produced by Alex G and Jacob Portrait, and all tracks were written by Alex Giannascoli.

Discogs lists Jacob Portrait as producer and mixer of the album. Mixing was at SugarHouse in NYC, and mastering was by Heba Kadry. Recording took place at several studios, including Clubhouse Recording Studios.
Alex G told NME that 'Blessing' was inspired by Audioslave.
The lyrics of 'Blessing' include biblical flood imagery. Alex G told NME he was drawn to the emotional weight of religious language.
Reviewers describe 'Blessing' as whispered vocals over cavernous synths. A guitar freak-out follows, and the song ends on a foreboding synth outro.
The album was the first Alex G record made solely in professional studios. One critic compared the whispery sound of 'Blessing' to 90s alt-grunge.
Alex G has said most of the album's God references were inspired by people close to him who recently became religious. He said writing the songs helped him explore what faith meant.

Alex G (Alexander Giannascoli) was born on February 3, 1993 in Havertown, Pennsylvania. He mostly records solo and is joined live by Sam Acchione, John Heywood and Tom Kelly, a lineup unchanged since 2016.

research.lineage: Alex G is a Philadelphia singer-songwriter who began in bedroom-recorded indie rock and later moved toward polished studio production. 'Blessing' pairs 90s alt-rock/grunge-style whispered vocals with experimental electronic textures.

draft:
Every line of **Blessing** arrives twice. Alex G says it, and something says it back: "Every day (every day) / Is a blessing (is a blessing)." On paper it reads like a congregation answering a preacher, the call-and-response of a church service. Sung in the whisper critics heard over cavernous synths, the echo sounds less like a crowd and more like a voice trying a phrase on to see if it holds weight. Repetition is how prayer works, and it's also how you talk yourself into something.

The words are almost a children's hymn. Mud, fishes, a flood. The image that matters is the conditional: "If I live (if I live) / Like the fishes (like the fishes)." The fish don't escape the flood. They belong to it. The salvation offered here is to stop fighting the water and become something that can breathe in it. That's a strange, slightly unsettling idea of grace, and the song never explains it. It just keeps repeating it.

Alex G has said most of the God references on *God Save the Animals* came from people close to him who had recently become religious, and that writing the songs helped him work out what faith meant. He also told NME he was drawn to the emotional weight of religious language. That's the feeling in "Blessing": standing just outside someone else's belief, borrowing its words, and finding they carry more than expected. Gratitude and dread share the same few lines. Calling every day a blessing while walking through mud is either faith or stubbornness, and the song leaves both possible. The little "huh" that slips in after "every day" and "through the mud" sounds like someone half-questioning what they just said.

He named Audioslave as an inspiration, which is a surprising touchstone for an artist who started out making bedroom-recorded indie rock in Philadelphia. One critic heard 90s alt-grunge in the whispered vocals, and the song reportedly breaks into a guitar freak-out before ending on a foreboding synth outro, so the blessing doesn't get the last word. This was the album's first single, released before the record was even announced. It was also the start of Alex G's first record made entirely in professional studios. Jacob Portrait engineered it at Clubhouse in Rhinebeck, New York, with Samuel Acchione on guitar, John Heywood on bass and Tom Kelly on drums. That's his touring band, together since 2016, finally playing on the record.

"Blessing" sticks because it hands you a comforting phrase and lets you feel how much fear it takes to keep saying it.
